title: Finding, Routing To, and Trusting a Server

questions.question: When a team publishes a server to the MCP Registry, what does the registry actually store?
options: A cached copy of every tool description the server has ever returned
A cryptographic attestation that the server's code contains no security vulnerabilities
The server's own runtime logs, kept so a client can audit past tool calls
Metadata that names, versions, and locates the server, not the server's own code
questions.explanation: The MCP Registry stores server.json metadata, name, version, and package or remote locations, and never hosts the server's own source code.

questions.question: A publisher who has never proven ownership of the io.github.acme account tries to publish a server named io.github.acme/reporting-tool. What does the registry do?
options: Rejects the publish, since that namespace belongs to another verified owner
Accepts the publish, since anyone may choose any name they like
Publishes it but marks the version string as a prohibited range
Silently reassigns the name to a namespace the publisher does control
questions.explanation: Namespace authentication ties a reverse DNS name to the specific GitHub account or domain that proved ownership of it, so a different publisher cannot claim it.

questions.question: A server.json's $schema field points at the 2025-12-11 schema revision. What does that date tell you about the server itself?
options: The server refuses connections unless their date matches 2025-12-11 exactly
Nothing; the schema date and the protocol version are tracked separately
The server speaks MCP protocol version 2025-12-11 at the wire level
The server will stop working once the 2026-07-28 revision ships
questions.explanation: A server.json's schema version describes the shape of the metadata document itself and is tracked completely separately from the MCP protocol version the server speaks at runtime.

questions.question: A gateway receives a request whose Mcp-Method header says prompts/get, but the JSON-RPC body's method field says tools/call. What must the gateway do?
options: Trust the header for routing and let the body's method execute unchanged
Execute the body's method first, then correct the header in its response
Reject the request as a header mismatch before any backend is reached
Fall back to a legacy session so the two methods can be reconciled
questions.explanation: Header and body must agree before a gateway routes or executes a request; a mismatch is rejected as HeaderMismatch with a 400 response before any backend is touched.

questions.question: Two different authenticated callers both request the same private scope resource through a gateway. What is the correct caching behavior?
options: The gateway never caches a private scope result for any caller at all
The gateway serves the second caller's request from the first caller's cached entry
The gateway serves both callers from cache once the first request completes
The gateway fetches the resource again for each caller and never shares that entry
questions.explanation: A private cacheScope result must never be shared across different callers, so the gateway fetches it again for each caller rather than reusing another caller's cached entry.

questions.question: An SDK rated Tier 1 then fails one conformance test on every run for five straight weeks. What happens to its tier?
options: It drops to Tier 2, since a sustained failure past four weeks relegates it
It stays at Tier 1, since one failing test is never enough to matter
It drops straight to Tier 3, since any conformance failure is treated as critical
It is removed from the tiering system until it is manually resubmitted
questions.explanation: An SDK is relegated only after a conformance test fails continuously for four full weeks; five weeks of failure crosses that threshold and drops Tier 1 to Tier 2.
